### Summary

If we defined a callback that updates the object before we defined the association, then this ivar may end up being manipulated to being `false` when it should be `true`. We guard this be only defining it once.

The implication of it being false, in this case, is that the children aren't updated with the parent_id and so they fail to associate with one another.

Fixes https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/38120

issue_context.title: If a callback is listed before an association and updates the parent, then parent_id is not assigned on children when parent is created
issue_context.body:
### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a has_many (children) and belongs_to (parent) relationship
2. Create a number of has_many children
3. Initialize the belongs_to parent with the children from (3) as the associations
4. Save the belongs_to parent, expect the children to have their `parent_id` column updated

**Important:** There are additional edge case steps listed in https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/38120#issuecomment-569822083 . You must have a callback listed before the `has_many` and the callback must `update` the parent in someway.

### Expected behavior

https://guides.rubyonrails.org/association_basics.html#has-many-association-reference-when-are-objects-saved-questionmark

> If the parent object (the one declaring the has_many association) is unsaved
> (that is, new_record? returns true) then the child objects are not saved when they are added.
> All unsaved members of the association will automatically be saved when the parent is saved.

The paragraph listed above lead me to believe that the `parent_id` of a child assigned before a parent is created (while `new_record?` would return true) would be nil until the parent is saved, then it would be updated such that the `parent_id` is the newly assigned id.

### Actual behavior

This was not the case, the parent had to be created first. I tried inverse_of and autosave, thinking those might help, but they didn't

[This Gist](https://gist.github.com/jules2689/62ab673933c3039baee3d773b0d2a047) has a snippet of code that reproduces what I mean

What's interesting is that until the parent is reloaded from the database, the `has_many` association is filled out as expected. Until you re-assign the has_many relationship, however, it will just be like an instance variable is assigned... nothing in the database side will change.

### Work Around

E.g. in a controller

```ruby
def create
  children =Children.where(id: parent_params.delete(:children_ids)
  parent = Parent.new(parent_params)
  if parent.save
    parent.children = children
    parent.save
    redirect_to parent_path(parent)
  else
    render "new"
  end
end
```

### System configuration
**Rails version**: `master`

**Ruby version**: `ruby 2.6.3p62 (2019-04-16 revision 67580) [universal.x86_64-darwin19]`
comments: Turns out my test was not resetting the DB between tests and it made it seem like I was hitting the same issue as my app, will keep digging but it looks like something is messing with the associations in a callback 😓

Aha! I figured it out. There is a series of weirdness to get this correct, and it is definitely an edge case. The gist has been updated to address this!

The state to replicate is:

1. Define an `after_create` callback **before** your `has_many` association (it could work with other associations and callbacks, but I did not check those)
2. In your callback, you have to **update an attribute**. This changes the record and the callbacks for the associations get confused

What I suspect is happening is that because associations rely on callbacks, but we are also defining a callback, we are getting a different order of callbacks in the internal array that keeps track of all callbacks.

When we define a callback _before_ our _has_many_, the _has_many_ callback is **after the user defined callback**. This is fine the majority of the time, however in my use case I was doing some logic elsewhere to create associations via API and automatically setup and calculate some attributes. This update meant that the `parent` is no longer "new" or "newly created" by the time we get to the `has_many` callbacks.

I think that a workaround fix would be to **ensure your associations are at the top of your model**, even before `include` statements for modules and concerns which may include callbacks.

I think that the ideal situation would be for callbacks to be treated equally somehow. A new record is still a new record despite being updated in a prior callback. That said, I can see how there would be conflicts with this method as we may have to keep track of an "original" copy of the model to check, otherwise we would not see the model updated between callbacks.

The issue is in this code: 
https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/4a17d3e045ef059d5c82d1ade4f7eae37bc1e485/activerecord/lib/active_record/autosave_association.rb#L365-L369

What happens is that on `create`, `@new_record_before_save` will be set to `true`. Then in your callback when you `update` the model, it is set again to `false`.

I suspect an easy fix would be to wrap that call in a `defined?` block, but I'm not sure what the implications of that would be for the nested call in `update` (to note, this is why I chose `after_create` as I assumed that this would be sufficient to avoid conflicting callbacks).

Interestingly enough, if I change `after_create` to any other callback then I get a `SystemStackError: stack level too deep` as Rails infinitely tries to save the associations.

Perhaps the lesson here is to not update attributes and instead assign before committing to the DB somehow.

```diff
diff --git a/activerecord/lib/active_record/autosave_association.rb b/activerecord/lib/active_record/autosave_association.rb
index 0c9c210bf2..cba294d54b 100644
--- a/activerecord/lib/active_record/autosave_association.rb
+++ b/activerecord/lib/active_record/autosave_association.rb
@@ -365,7 +365,9 @@ def normalize_reflection_attribute(indexed_attribute, reflection, index, attribu
       # Is used as a before_save callback to check while saving a collection
       # association whether or not the parent was a new record before saving.
       def before_save_collection_association
-        @new_record_before_save = new_record?
+        unless defined?(@new_record_before_save)
+          @new_record_before_save = new_record?
+        end
       end
 
       def after_save_collection_association
diff --git a/guides/source/active_record_callbacks.md b/guides/source/active_record_callbacks.md
index 1518c704ff..e9df505f21 100644
--- a/guides/source/active_record_callbacks.md
+++ b/guides/source/active_record_callbacks.md
@@ -117,6 +117,8 @@ Here is a list with all the available Active Record callbacks, listed in the sam
 
 WARNING. `after_save` runs both on create and update, but always _after_ the more specific callbacks `after_create` and `after_update`, no matter the order in which the macro calls were executed.
 
+WARNING. Care should be taken in callbacks to avoid updating attributes. For example, avoid running `update(attribute: "value")` and similar code during callbacks. This can alter the state of the model and may result in unexpected side effects during commit. Instead, you should try to assign values in the `before_create` or earlier callbacks.
+
 NOTE: `before_destroy` callbacks should be placed before `dependent: :destroy`
 associations (or use the `prepend: true` option), to ensure they execute before
 the records are deleted by `dependent: :destroy`.
```

Here is a suggested change. The first file fixes the Gist attached to this issue. The second file adds a warning to the docs to suggest people assign attributes instead of updating them during callbacks.

review_comments:
Not sure if I get this fix. This instance variable is only set on associations callback so I don't see how `@new_record_before_save` would be defined when the `before_save_collection_association ` is called. Could you explain?

I can see how `new_record?` return `false` if a callback before this one salved the record, but if no other `before_save_collection_association` have run yet the `@new_record_before_save` should not be defined.

The linked issue has more details, but I'll go into it a bit more here too :)

autosave associations works on a before_save. What I was experiencing is that in the case where a callback is defined before the has many (and that callback updates the model), then the children records would never get updated with the parent id.

This is because the following would happen:

1. Record create called
2. Autosave's Before save called and sets ivar to true
3. After create called and updates the record
4. Autosave's Before save gets called a second time and is no longer true
5. We try to set the parent id on the children, but the ivar is false.

If we set the ivar only once, then it is unaffected in subsequent callbacks and we will only take the initial value.

In my case I had been updating a model in an after create with some computations, which is when I noticed my children models weren't associating anymore.

I had hoped to discuss the implications of such a change like this, as I'm not fully aware of what it could imply to other parts of the codebase. It is also interesting to note that updating in most other callbacks create an infinite loop of saving, this one and any after it (e.g. after commit) are the only ones in which updating is possible.
Oh also! There is a bug test case linked in the issue that reproduces the issue ☺️ maybe that will help too!
Ok. This change now makes sense to me.
